findings.reason: every one of the twenty leak fixtures does carry a structural opening (regex hits 35–93 each, 20 of 20 fixtures), so the plan can and should require exactly twenty firings; as written a matcher that misses, say, five leaks still satisfies the measure, and §5's whole success claim rests on the guard firing on every leak.
findings.text: s3's population-pass measure is conditional and therefore unfalsifiable over the known leaks: it requires the log to list "one [firing] for each leaked call whose argument carries a structural opening"

findings.reason: a guard that never fires on the real stream is the whole fix failing silently (the leak class §1 measured stays, and §5's post-restart census would then read zero leaks from an unproven cause); the plan needs either the watch to match the reassembled-and-`json`-decoded input, or one captured real SSE frame to fix the encoding before the relay tests are built on the assumption.
findings.text: s3 matches the DSML opening in the accumulated `input_json_delta` text, but nothing in the plan establishes that the serve's SSE carries the token literally rather than JSON-unicode-escaped, and both its instruments (the relay test and the population pass) synthesise deltas from the decoded tool input, so a `<`-escaped serve yields no firing in production with every test green

findings.reason: §5 (depends-on s3) measures "the number of firings and of pass-throughs" from those lines, so if §3 leaves the destination unnamed that measure has no readable source; s3 is the changed unit that introduces the instrument, so the path belongs here.
findings.text: s3 states "the router writes one log line per firing … and that line is what a census counts" but names no durable path, and the router's only log sink is a `logging` StreamHandler on the serving process's stdout (router.py L3025–3037)
